stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the blue swatch?
stimulus: Synthetic dyes were first produced in 1856, so textile historians can often date a fabric by testing its colorants. A newly catalogued set of 214 swatches from an English mill mostly meets expectations: nearly all contain synthetic dyes, which fits the mill's records of weaving them in the 1870s. One blue swatch, however, contains only natural indigo. The mill's ledgers show that it had switched to synthetic blue by 1868, so researchers suspect the swatch was cut from older stock rather than woven alongside the rest.
choices: It contains synthetic colorants, as do nearly all of the swatches in the set.
It was likely made earlier than most of the set, though it was kept with 1870s cloth.
It shows that the mill never used synthetic dyes when producing its blue cloth.
It was woven in the 1870s with natural indigo the mill purchased after 1868.
explanation: Put together every sentence about the blue swatch. It contains only natural indigo, the mill had switched to synthetic blue by 1868, and researchers suspect it came from older stock. Together these mean it was probably made before the rest of the set, even though it was stored with cloth from the 1870s. Choice B states that consequence and stops there.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Nearly all the swatches contain synthetic dyes, but the passage singles out the blue one because it contains only natural indigo.

C.why: You stretched one swatch into a claim about everything the mill made. The ledgers actually show the mill was using synthetic blue by 1868, so the text points the other way.

D.why: You mixed up the dates. Researchers think the swatch was not woven in the 1870s with the rest, and nothing says the mill bought natural indigo after 1868, the year by which it had switched to synthetic blue.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the Corran Bridge?
stimulus: Most suspension bridges built in the Calder region during the 1930s used shallow stiffening girders, a choice that kept them light and inexpensive. The Corran Bridge was an exception. Its engineers insisted on a deep open truss, which raised the bridge's weight and cost by nearly a fifth. However, when a severe windstorm struck in 1950, several neighboring spans twisted so badly that they had to be closed, while the Corran Bridge needed only minor repairs.
choices: It used a shallow girder like nearby spans, but it was repaired more quickly.
It became the model for every suspension bridge built in the region after 1950.
Its truss made it lighter than nearby spans, which reduced its twisting in wind.
Its deep truss increased its cost but also helped it come through a severe storm.
explanation: The text tells you two things about the Corran Bridge's deep truss. It added nearly a fifth to the cost, and after the 'However' pivot, the bridge needed only minor repairs when nearby spans failed. Choice D joins the drawback and the benefit of that one feature.

A.why: You gave the exception the group's feature. The other bridges used shallow girders. The Corran Bridge is set apart precisely because it used a deep truss.

B.why: This sounds like a natural next step, but the passage says nothing about later bridges copying the Corran design.

C.why: You got the weight backward. The truss made the bridge heavier, not lighter. The shallow girders were the light option.

stem: What does the text indicate about the Halvern district?
stimulus: The 1962 master plan for the city of Delmont separated residential, commercial, and industrial land into distinct zones, and nearly every district built under it followed that rule. The Halvern district did not. Because its land had been subdivided before the plan was adopted, planners allowed its existing ground-floor shops beneath apartments to remain. Recent travel surveys suggest that Halvern residents make fewer car trips for errands than residents of any other Delmont district.
choices: Its mixed uses predate the plan, and its residents seem to drive less for errands.
It kept housing and shops in separate zones, as the plan required of every district.
Its example led planners to abandon zoning separation throughout the rest of Delmont.
It was subdivided after 1962, so planners designed it with shops beneath apartments.
explanation: Collect the Halvern sentences. Its shops beneath apartments were already there before the 1962 plan, and surveys suggest its residents make fewer car trips for errands. Choice A combines both facts and keeps the hedge, since 'seem' matches 'suggest'.

B.why: You described the rule the rest of the city followed. Halvern is the district that did not separate housing from shops.

C.why: The passage never says Halvern changed how the rest of Delmont was zoned. This choice invents a consequence the text does not support.

D.why: You reversed the order of events. The land was subdivided before the plan, and planners allowed existing shops to remain rather than designing new ones.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the lung-resident memory B cells?
stimulus: Most memory B cells produced after a vaccination circulate in the blood for months and then gradually decline. In a study of mice immunized against an influenza strain, however, researchers found a small population of these cells that had settled in lung tissue itself. The lung-resident cells were far fewer than the circulating ones, but when the mice were later exposed to the virus, they began producing antibodies days sooner. The researchers concluded that location, rather than number, may matter most for early protection.
choices: They circulated in the blood for months and then declined, as most memory cells do.
They gave the immunized mice complete protection against every strain of influenza.
Though fewer than the circulating cells, they began making antibodies days sooner.
They outnumbered the circulating cells, which explains their faster antibody response.
explanation: The text describes the lung-resident cells in two ways. They were 'far fewer' than the circulating cells, and they produced antibodies 'days sooner.' Choice C combines that contrast: small in number, but faster.

A.why: You described the typical memory cell, not the exception. The passage sets the lung-resident cells apart from cells that circulate and decline.

B.why: The study tested one influenza strain and measured how quickly antibodies appeared. It never claims complete protection, let alone protection against every strain.

D.why: You confused speed with number. The cells were faster but far fewer, which is exactly why the researchers credited location rather than number.

stem: What does the text indicate about the chart attributed to the Genoese workshop?
stimulus: Sixteenth-century portolan charts generally recorded coastlines in remarkable detail while leaving the interiors of continents blank. A chart attributed to a Genoese workshop is unusual in this respect: it fills the interior of North Africa with rivers and towns. Comparison with travelers' accounts, however, shows that many of those inland features are misplaced by hundreds of kilometers, even though the chart's coastline is as accurate as that of any contemporary chart.
choices: Like other charts of its time, it leaves the interior of North Africa blank.
Unlike most charts of its time, it depicts the interior, though often inaccurately.
Its coastline is badly misplaced, while its interior rivers and towns are accurate.
It was the chart most widely consulted by Mediterranean navigators of its era.
explanation: Two sentences describe this chart. It is unusual because it fills in the interior, and many of those inland features are misplaced. Choice B combines its difference from other charts with the problem in what it adds.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Most charts left the interior blank. This one is notable because it does not.

C.why: You swapped the two features. The coastline is accurate and the interior features are misplaced, not the other way around.

D.why: This sounds like a scholarly fact, but the passage never says anything about how widely the chart was used.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Kesselopteris arcana?
stimulus: Most plant fossils recovered from the Kessel shale belong to genera that still have living relatives, which lets researchers estimate the ancient climate from where those relatives grow today. A fern identified in the shale in 2021, Kesselopteris arcana, cannot be used this way. Its leaves combine structural features of two separate fern families, a combination found in no living fern, and the species is known only from fossils preserved in the shale.
choices: It appears to be extinct, so it offers no modern range for inferring climate.
It belongs to a genus whose living relatives reveal the shale's ancient climate.
It is the most frequently studied fossil fern recovered from the Kessel shale.
It belongs to one of two living fern families, though its leaves are unusual.
explanation: Combine the facts. The fern is known only from fossils, and no living fern shares its leaf structure, so it appears to be extinct. That is why it 'cannot be used this way': it has no living relatives whose range could point to a climate. Choice A states this small logical consequence.

B.why: You described the rest of the fossils, not the exception. The passage introduces this fern as the one that cannot be used to estimate climate.

C.why: 'Frequently studied' sounds scientific, but nothing in the text says how often the fern has been studied. It was only identified in 2021.

D.why: You misread the category. The fern combines features of two families, a combination no living fern has. The text never places it in either family.

stem: What does the text indicate about Dunmore Spring?
stimulus: Springs fed by shallow aquifers typically shrink within weeks of a drought's onset, because the water they release fell as rain only recently. Dunmore Spring, in an otherwise drought-sensitive valley, kept flowing steadily through a fourteen-month dry spell. Isotope analysis indicates that its water entered the ground roughly 3,000 years ago, suggesting that the spring draws on a deep aquifer rather than on the shallow ones that feed its neighbors.
choices: Like nearby springs, it is fed by recent rainfall held in a shallow aquifer.
Its flow will remain unaffected by any future drought, however long it lasts.
Its water fell as rain recently, which let it recover quickly after the drought.
Its water likely comes from a deep source, which helps explain its steady flow.
explanation: Gather the sentences about Dunmore Spring. It kept flowing through a long drought, and its water is about 3,000 years old, 'suggesting' a deep aquifer. Choice D links the deep source to the steady flow and keeps the hedge with 'likely'.

A.why: You described the neighboring springs. The text sets Dunmore apart from springs fed by recent rain in shallow aquifers.

B.why: The spring survived one fourteen-month dry spell. The text gives no basis for predicting it will survive every future drought.

C.why: You got the water's age wrong. It entered the ground about 3,000 years ago, and the spring never stopped flowing, so there was nothing to recover from.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the warbler population that nests in the geothermal valley?
stimulus: Nearly all populations of the gray-crowned warbler leave their northern breeding grounds each autumn and spend the winter in Central America. Banding records show that one population, nesting along a geothermal river valley in the Rockies, is an exception: its members remain through the winter, feeding on insects that stay active near the warm water. That same dependence, however, leaves the population vulnerable. In years when the valley's hot springs weaken, its numbers drop sharply.
choices: It spends winter in Central America, as the species' other populations do.
It migrates north each autumn to feed on insects near the valley's hot springs.
The warm water that lets it stay through winter also leaves it open to decline.
It is growing faster than other populations because it avoids risky migration.
explanation: The passage names one factor, the valley's warm water, and gives it two effects. It lets the birds stay through winter by keeping insects active, and it exposes them to sharp declines when the springs weaken. Choice C is the only one that combines both.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Other populations winter in Central America. This one stays put.

B.why: You treated a question of whether the birds migrate as a question of which direction they go. This population does not migrate at all. It remains in the valley through the winter.

D.why: The text never compares growth rates, and it actually stresses that this population is vulnerable. The claim about faster growth is invented.
